claim: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide.
source: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide and comprise a range of syndromes affecting the functionality of the heart and blood vessels (Smolders et al., 2018; Townsend et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smolders et al., 2018 and Townsend et al., 2022

claim: Vascular dysfunction is believed to be a primary factor in the onset and progression of atherosclerosis and other vascular-related disorders.
source: Vascular dysfunction is believed to be a primary factor in the onset and progression of atherosclerosis and other vascular-related disorders.
evidence: Draws from established scientific understanding in the field

claim: AMI is a major cause of morbidity in the Western world.
source: In this study, we focus our attention on a specific vascular disease, AMI, a major cause of morbidity in the Western world (Townsend et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Townsend et al., 2022

claim: AMI occurs as a consequence of coronary occlusion, generally from a thrombus superimposed on an ulcerated or unstable atherosclerotic plaque.
source: AMI occurs as a consequence of coronary occlusion, generally from a thrombus superimposed on an ulcerated or unstable atherosclerotic plaque (Badimon et al., 2012; Smolders et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Badimon et al., 2012 and Smolders et al., 2018

claim: The endothelium plays a pivotal role in the development of AMI, both preceding atherogenesis and predisposing to thrombosis.
source: The endothelium plays a pivotal role in the development of AMI, both preceding atherogenesis and predisposing to thrombosis (Previtali et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Previtali et al., 2011

claim: Pathological blood vessel responses and endothelial dysfunction are associated with metabolic alterations in ECs.
source: Emerging evidence indicates that pathological blood vessel responses and endothelial dysfunction are associated with metabolic alterations in ECs (Botts et al., 2021; Moreno-Viedma et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Botts et al., 2021 and Moreno-Viedma et al., 2016

claim: AMIECs were isolated from coronary atherothrombotic specimens from eight patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention with thrombectomy for the treatment of acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
source: AMIECs were isolated from coronary atherothrombotic specimens from eight patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention with thrombectomy for the treatment of acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
evidence: Describes the experimental methodology used in the study

claim: At 80% confluence, AMIECs presented the expected shape and appeared similar to control HCAECs.
source: At 80% confluence, AMIECs presented the expected shape and appeared similar to control HCAECs (Figure 1A), as expected for bonafide endothelial cells grown under equivalent conditions.
evidence: Supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 1A

claim: The endothelial nature of AMIECs was confirmed by Western blotting for the expression of the endothelial markers, V-CAM1, PECAM-1, CD-34, and CD-105.
source: The endothelial nature of these cells was confirmed by Western blotting for the expression of the endothelial markers, V-CAM1 (vascular cell adhesion protein 1, CD-106), PECAM-1 (platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule, CD31), CD-34, and CD-105 (endoglin) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: All AMIECs consistently displayed slower growth rates as compared to control HCAECs.
source: Under these conditions, all AMIECs consistently displayed slower growth rates as compared to control HCAECs (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 1D

claim: After 168 hr, while control HCAECs had reached a plateau in their growth, AMIECs continued to proliferate exponentially, albeit at slow rates, without reaching saturation.
source: Indeed, after 168 hr, while control HCAECs had reached a plateau in their growth, AMIECs continued to proliferate exponentially, albeit at slow rates, without reaching saturation.
evidence: Based on observations from growth monitoring experiments

claim: No significant differences were observed in the distribution of cell cycle phases between AMIECs and control cells.
source: Somewhat contrary to our expectations, we observed no significant differences in the distribution of cell cycle phases between AMIECs and control cells (Figure 1E), except for a modest tendency, without reaching statistical significance, of AMIECs to accumulate in the G1 phase relative to HCAECs.
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The slow growth rate, in conjunction with unaltered cell cycle phase distribution, of AMIECs suggests an overall slowing down of growth that affects equally all phases of the cell cycle.
source: The slow growth rate, in conjunction with unaltered cell cycle phase distribution, of AMIECs suggests an overall slowing down of growth that affects equally all phases of the cell cycle.
evidence: Inference drawn from the combination of growth rate and cell cycle distribution data

claim: Control HCAECs achieved a complete closure of the wound after 24 hr of seeding in wound-healing migration assays.
source: In wound-healing migration assays, control HCAECs achieved a complete closure of the wound after 24 hr of seeding (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Three AMIECs displayed wound closure rates below 50%, four others about 60%, and only one about 80% after 24 hr of migration.
source: In contrast, three AMIECs displayed wound closure rates below 50%, four others about 60%, and only one about 80% after 24 hr of migration under the same conditions (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 1G

claim: AMI patient-derived coronary endothelial cells are dysfunctional in major cell-autonomous processes, namely growth and migration.
source: These results indicate that AMI patient-derived coronary endothelial cells are dysfunctional in major cell-autonomous processes, namely growth and migration.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the growth and migration data presented

claim: Impairment in migration is considered a hallmark of vascular diseases.
source: Impairment in this fundamental endothelial function is considered a hallmark of vascular diseases (De Bock et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to De Bock et al., 2013

claim: Control HCAECs averaged 80 branching points in tubulogenesis assays.
source: While control HCAECs averaged 80 branching points, AMIECs displayed a significantly reduced tubulogenic potential, evident both as a diminished number of branching points and as shorter and fragmented tubes as compared to control cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by tubulogenesis assay data shown in Figure 2B

claim: AMIECs displayed a significantly reduced tubulogenic potential, evident both as a diminished number of branching points and as shorter and fragmented tubes as compared to control cells.
source: While control HCAECs averaged 80 branching points, AMIECs displayed a significantly reduced tubulogenic potential, evident both as a diminished number of branching points and as shorter and fragmented tubes as compared to control cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by tubulogenesis assay data shown in Figure 2A and 2B

claim: The branching capacity of the AMIECs derived from different patients was linearly correlated (R2=0.67) with their ability to migrate.
source: The branching capacity of the AMIECs derived from different patients was linearly correlated (R2=0.67) with their ability to migrate (Figure 2C) regardless of their growth rates suggesting that the deficient tubulogenesis or sprouting of these cells is linked to a defect in their migration properties, rather than to abnormal proliferation or survival.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: The deficient tubulogenesis or sprouting of AMIECs is linked to a defect in their migration properties, rather than to abnormal proliferation or survival.
source: The branching capacity of the AMIECs derived from different patients was linearly correlated (R2=0.67) with their ability to migrate (Figure 2C) regardless of their growth rates suggesting that the deficient tubulogenesis or sprouting of these cells is linked to a defect in their migration properties, rather than to abnormal proliferation or survival.
evidence: Inference drawn from the correlation between migration and tubulogenesis data

claim: Six out of the 8 AMIECs consumed glucose at significantly lower rates than control HCAECs.
source: We found that 6 out of the 8 AMIECs consumed glucose at significantly lower rates than control HCAECs (Figure 3A), which may reconcile with the lower growth rates of patient-derived cells, while two patient-derived cell lines consumed more glucose than control cells.
evidence: Supported by glucose consumption measurements shown in Figure 3A

claim: All AMIECs displayed a strong production of lactate, comparable or superior to control cells, regardless of their levels of glucose uptake.
source: Remarkably, all AMIECs displayed a strong production of lactate, comparable or superior to control cells, regardless of their levels of glucose uptake (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by lactate production measurements shown in Figure 3B

claim: Two of the AMIECs, CE-45, and CE-61, consumed high levels of glucose and displayed robust lactate production.
source: Two of the AMIECs, CE-45, and CE-61, consumed high levels of glucose and displayed robust lactate production (Figure 3A and B), and thus, it may be assumed that lactate is produced through glycolysis.
evidence: Supported by glucose and lactate measurements shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: The uncoupling of lactate production from glycolysis suggests the existence of an alternative source of lactate in AMIECs.
source: This uncoupling of lactate production from glycolysis suggests the existence of an alternative source of lactate in these cells.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation of high lactate production despite low glucose consumption

claim: Glutaminolysis produces lactate in a pathway that involves the oxidation of glutamine to malate and then to pyruvate by the malic enzyme (ME), followed by conversion to lactate by the action of LDH-A.
source: In this regard, it is worth noting that glutaminolysis also produces lactate, in a pathway that involves the oxidation of glutamine to malate and then to pyruvate by the malic enzyme (ME), followed by conversion to lactate by the action of LDH-A (Brooks, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brooks, 2018

claim: Under normal conditions, endothelial cells rely mainly on glycolysis to generate the energy required for their functions.
source: Under normal conditions, endothelial cells rely mainly on glycolysis to generate the energy required for their functions (De Bock et al., 2013; Dromparis and Michelakis, 2013; Goveia et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Bock et al., 2013; Dromparis and Michelakis, 2013; Goveia et al., 2014

claim: PFKFB3 has been described to play a significant role in the glycolytic activity of pathological ECs, and its inhibition dramatically abrogates their proliferation and migration.
source: PFKFB3 has been described to play a significant role in the glycolytic activity of pathological ECs, and its inhibition dramatically abrogates their proliferation and migration (Li et al., 2019; Schoors et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2019 and Schoors et al., 2014

claim: Seven out of the 8 AMIECs expressed significantly lower levels of PFKFB3 protein than control HCAECs.
source: We determined PFKFB3 protein levels by Western blotting, finding significantly lower levels in 7 out of the 8 AMIECs, as compared to control HCAECs (Figure 4A and B), consistent with their lower glucose uptake.
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: AMIECs expressed significantly higher levels of PFKFB4 protein compared to control cells.
source: We also determined PFKFB4 protein levels, finding significantly higher levels of expression in AMIECs compared to control cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: Low levels of PFKFB3 expression coupled with high levels of PFKFB4 expression in AMI patient-derived cells predict a redirection of glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) towards the PPP.
source: Low levels of PFKFB3 expression coupled with high levels of PFKFB4 expression in AMI patient-derived cells predict a redirection of glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) towards the PPP.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed expression patterns of PFKFB3 and PFKFB4

claim: AMIECs expressed significantly higher levels of G6PD than control cells.
source: Consistently, we found significantly higher levels of G6PD in AMIECs than in control cells (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: AMIECs displayed higher levels of G6PD enzyme activity than control cells.
source: Likewise, AMIECs displayed higher levels of G6PD enzyme activity than control cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 4E

claim: Seven out of the 8 AMIECs contained ROS at significantly higher levels than control cells.
source: Seven out of the 8 AMIECs contained ROS at significantly higher levels than control cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by ROS measurements shown in Figure 4F

claim: The intracellular concentration of reduced glutathione was increased in all 8 AMIECs.
source: Similarly, the intracellular concentration of reduced glutathione was increased in all 8 AMIECs (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by glutathione measurements shown in Figure 4G

claim: Glutathione levels are upregulated in AMIECs to counter excess ROS levels.
source: These observations suggest that glutathione levels are upregulated in AMIECs to counter excess ROS levels.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed high levels of both ROS and glutathione

claim: The high levels of ROS in AIM patient-derived cells may be elicited by endogenous damage signals impinging upon mitochondria or through NAD(P)H oxidases.
source: Absent maintenance of long-term epigenetic memory of past stress responses in vivo, it is reasonable to assume that the high levels of ROS in AIM patient-derived cells may be elicited by endogenous damage signals impinging upon mitochondria (Murphy, 2009) or through NAD(P)H oxidases.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observation of high ROS levels in cultured cells, with citation to Murphy, 2009

claim: The consumption of glutamine in AMIECs is higher than in control HCAECs.
source: Determination of the extracellular fluxes of glutamine showed that the consumption of glutamine in AMIECs is higher than in control HCAECs (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by glutamine consumption measurements shown in Figure 5A

claim: The glutamine-to-glucose consumption ratio is far greater in patient-derived cells than in control cells.
source: The latter consumed more glucose than patient-derived cells (see above), and thus the glutamine-to-glucose consumption ratio is far greater in patient-derived cells than in control cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Inference drawn from the comparison of glutamine and glucose consumption data shown in Figure 5B

claim: AMI patient-derived cells mainly resort to glutamine, rather than glucose, as their carbon source.
source: This suggests that AMI patient-derived cells mainly resort to glutamine, rather than glucose, as their carbon source.
evidence: Inference drawn from the high glutamine-to-glucose consumption ratio

claim: Both isoforms of GLS1, KGA, and GAC, are expressed at significantly higher levels in patient-derived cells than control cells.
source: Consistently, both isoforms of GLS1, KGA, and GAC, are expressed at significantly higher levels in patient-derived cells than control cells (Figure 5B and C), with a higher KGA/GAC ratio in AMIECs (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 5B and C

claim: AMIECs have a higher KGA/GAC ratio than control cells.
source: Consistently, both isoforms of GLS1, KGA, and GAC, are expressed at significantly higher levels in patient-derived cells than control cells (Figure 5B and C), with a higher KGA/GAC ratio in AMIECs (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5D

claim: All amino acids determined had higher intracellular content in AMIECs, with the exception of glycine, alanine, histidine, and proline.
source: The results disclosed a higher intracellular content of all amino acids determined, with the exception of glycine, alanine, histidine, and proline.
evidence: Based on GC/MS analysis of intracellular metabolites

claim: Cysteine and glutamate had significantly higher concentrations in all AMIECs.
source: Cysteine and glutamate play important roles in the synthesis of glutathione (GSH) (Ishimoto et al., 2011) and both had significantly higher concentrations in all AMIECs (Figure 5E), consistent with higher levels of GSH as compared to control cells.
evidence: Supported by intracellular amino acid measurements shown in Figure 5E, with citation to Ishimoto et al., 2011

claim: Six out of the 8 patient-derived cells showed lower levels of glutamate production as compared to control cells.
source: We thus determined glutamate levels in culture media, finding lower levels of production in 6 out of the 8 patient-derived cells as compared to control cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by glutamate production measurements shown in Figure 5F

claim: The ratio between glutamate production and glutamine consumption was considerably lower in AMIECs.
source: Moreover, the ratio between glutamate production and glutamine consumption was considerably lower in AMIECs (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by ratio calculations shown in Figure 5G

claim: The lower levels of extracellular export of glutamate are suggestive of a robust consumption of glutamate in the production of GSH in AMIECs.
source: Because of the high levels of glutaminase in patient-derived cells, implying a strong conversion of glutamine to glutamate, the lower levels of extracellular export of glutamate are suggestive of a robust consumption of glutamate in the production of GSH in these cells.
evidence: Inference drawn from the combination of high glutaminase levels and low glutamate export

claim: AMIECs rely heavily on glutamine, both as an alternative to glucose as a carbon source and in order to maintain redox homeostasis in these cells.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that AMIECs rely heavily on glutamine, both as an alternative to glucose as a carbon source and in order to maintain redox homeostasis in these cells.
evidence: Inference drawn from the collective metabolic data on glutamine consumption and metabolism

claim: A link between glutamine metabolism and clinical manifestations of atherosclerosis, such as intima-media thickness and plaque development, has been described.
source: Related to our observations, a link between glutamine metabolism and clinical manifestations of atherosclerosis, such as intima-media thickness and plaque development, has been described (Grajeda-Iglesias and Aviram, 2018; Wurtz et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grajeda-Iglesias and Aviram, 2018 and Wurtz et al., 2012

claim: Aspartate was found at increased levels in AMIECs.
source: Consistently, aspartate was found at increased levels in AMIECs (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by intracellular metabolite measurements shown in Figure 5E

claim: All AMIECs accumulated MitoProbe at significantly higher levels relative to control HCAECs, indicating a mitochondrial hyperpolarization due to increased membrane potentials.
source: MitoProbe accumulated at significantly higher levels in all AMIECs relative to control HCAECs (Figure 5H), indicating a mitochondrial hyperpolarization due to increased membrane potentials.
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial membrane potential measurements shown in Figure 5H

claim: The subsequent addition of the uncoupling agent carbonyl cyanide m-chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP) resulted in rapid depolarization, reflecting the proton gradient dissipation.
source: The subsequent addition of the uncoupling agent carbonyl cyanide m-chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP) resulted in rapid depolarization, reflecting the proton gradient dissipation.
evidence: Based on experimental observations with CCCP treatment

claim: Contrary to physiologically normal ECs, which rely mostly on glycolysis for energy production rather than mitochondrial respiration, AMIECs display low levels of glycolysis.
source: We have found that contrary to physiologically normal ECs, which rely mostly on glycolysis for energy production rather than mitochondrial respiration (Krützfeldt et al., 1990), AMIECs display low levels of glycolysis, as attested by low glucose consumption and downregulation of PFKFB3, which catalyzes the production of fructose-2,6-bisP (F2,6BP), a potent allosteric activator of the glycolysis rate-limiting enzyme 6-phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1), while also displaying a high membrane potential, suggestive of a high mitochondrial activity.
evidence: Inference drawn from the collective metabolic data, with citation to Krützfeldt et al., 1990

claim: AMIECs display a high intracellular content of ROS consistent with high levels of mitochondrial activity.
source: Consistent with high levels of mitochondrial activity, AMIECs display a high intracellular content of ROS.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed high ROS levels and high mitochondrial membrane potential

claim: The combination of high membrane potential and high ROS levels suggests robust proton coupling at the inner mitochondrial membrane in AMIECs.
source: The combination of high membrane potential and high ROS levels suggests robust proton coupling at the inner mitochondrial membrane, as uncoupling through the expression of UCP1 or the use of pharmacological uncouplers has been shown to mitigate ROS production (Cadenas, 2018).
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed high membrane potential and high ROS levels, with citation to Cadenas, 2018

claim: The augmented ROS content is counteracted in AMIECs by an augmented intracellular content of glutathione.
source: We have found that the augmented ROS content is counteracted in AMIECs by an augmented intracellular content of glutathione, a physiological homeostatic mechanism to prevent damage from excess ROS (Hayes et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed high levels of both ROS and glutathione, with citation to Hayes et al., 2020

claim: The major pathways enabling the biosynthesis of glutathione, the PPP and glutaminolysis, are overactivated in AIMECs as compared to control coronary ECs.
source: We also provide evidence that the major pathways enabling the biosynthesis of glutathione, the PPP and glutaminolysis, are overactivated in AIMECs as compared to control coronary ECs.
evidence: Inference drawn from the collective data on G6PD, PFKFB4, and glutaminase expression and activity

claim: The relatively low levels of expression of PFKFB3 and high levels of PFKFB4 point to a shunting of glycolysis towards the PPP in AMIECs, in order to produce NADPH.
source: The relatively low levels of expression of PFKFB3 and high levels of PFKFB4 point to a shunting of glycolysis towards the PPP in AMIECs, in order to produce NADPH.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed expression patterns of PFKFB3 and PFKFB4

claim: Both PFKFB4 and PFKFB3 are upregulated in hypoxia through transcriptional activation by HIF-1α, the mTOR pathway, and peroxisome proliferator-activating receptor γ (PPARγ).
source: Both PFKFB4 and PFKFB3 are upregulated in hypoxia through transcriptional activation by HIF-1α (Minchenko et al., 2014), the mTOR pathway (Feng and Wu, 2017), and peroxisome proliferator-activating receptor γ (PPARγ) (Shu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Minchenko et al., 2014; Feng and Wu, 2017; and Shu et al., 2016

claim: Wild-type p53, activated in response to DNA damage, transcriptionally represses both PFKFB3 and PFKFB4.
source: On the other hand, although wild-type p53, activated in response to DNA damage, transcriptionally represses both PFKFB3 and PFKFB4, PFKFB4, but not PFKFB3, has been described as strongly upregulated in the absence of p53 (Ros et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ros et al., 2017

claim: PFKFB4, but not PFKFB3, has been described as strongly upregulated in the absence of p53.
source: On the other hand, although wild-type p53, activated in response to DNA damage, transcriptionally represses both PFKFB3 and PFKFB4, PFKFB4, but not PFKFB3, has been described as strongly upregulated in the absence of p53 (Ros et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ros et al., 2017

claim: The malic enzyme isoforms, ME1 and ME2, are under negative regulation by p53 and are upregulated in the absence of p53.
source: Interestingly, the malic enzyme isoforms, ME1 and ME2, are also under negative regulation by p53 and are upregulated in the absence of p53 (Ros et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ros et al., 2017

claim: PFKFB4 activates steroid receptor coactivator-3 (SRC-3), enhancing its transcriptional activity and stimulating the expression of transketolase (TKT).
source: Regardless of the mechanisms underlying PFKFB3 low-expression along with PFKFB4 over-expression in AMIECs, predicted downstream consequences are (1) decreased levels of F-2,6-P2 resulting in low PFK1 activity and diminished glycolytic flux, which is consistent with the observed phenotypes, and (2) shunting of G6P towards the PPP, reinforced by the activation by PFKFB4 of steroid receptor coactivator-3 (SRC-3), enhancing its transcriptional activity and stimulating the expression of transketolase (TKT) (Dasgupta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dasgupta et al., 2018

claim: High lactate production is frequently linked to strong glycolytic activity.
source: High lactate production is frequently linked to strong glycolytic activity, as the glycolytic end-product, pyruvate, can be converted to lactate catalyzed by the enzymatic activity of lactate dehydrogenase-A (LDH-A).
evidence: Draws from established biochemical knowledge

claim: In highly proliferating cells, such as cancer or progenitor cells, a high rate of glycolysis can be accompanied by an inhibition of the mitochondrial entry of pyruvate, which, instead, is diverted towards the generation of lactate, a metabolic rewiring designated the Warburg effect, or aerobic glycolysis.
source: Indeed, in highly proliferating cells, such as cancer or progenitor cells, a high rate of glycolysis can be accompanied by an inhibition of the mitochondrial entry of pyruvate, which, instead, is diverted towards the generation of lactate, a metabolic rewiring designated the Warburg effect, or aerobic glycolysis (Burns and Manda, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burns and Manda, 2017

claim: Strong glycolysis coupled with high lactate production and mitochondrial shutdown is characteristic of hypoxia, through transcriptional regulation by HIF-1α.
source: Strong glycolysis coupled with high lactate production and mitochondrial shutdown is also characteristic of hypoxia, through transcriptional regulation by HIF-1α of key regulators of these three processes, and has been observed in dysfunctional endothelial cells associated with atherosclerosis and vascular diseases (Fitzgerald et al., 2018; Theodorou and Boon, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fitzgerald et al., 2018 and Theodorou and Boon, 2018

claim: In the LDH-A catalyzed reaction, pyruvate accepts electrons from NADH, yielding lactate and replenishing NAD+.
source: In the LDH-A catalyzed reaction, pyruvate accepts electrons from NADH, yielding lactate and replenishing NAD+, predicted to be depleted in AMIECs by a strong drive to produce reducing equivalents and by the increased mitochondrial membrane potential, which impairs electron transport and NAD + regeneration (Luengo et al., 2021).
evidence: Draws from established biochemical knowledge, with citation to Luengo et al., 2021

claim: Glutamine-initiated metabolism can produce lactate from pyruvate.
source: However, under conditions of low glucose consumption and evidence of low glycolytic activity, an alternative source is needed that may explain high lactate production from pyruvate in AMIECs. One possibility is through glutamine-initiated metabolism (Zielke et al., 1980), which would be consistent with the strong glutamine consumption observed in AMIECs.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zielke et al., 1980

claim: Glutamine-derived pyruvate plays a significant role in redox homeostasis in pancreatic cancer cells.
source: In this regard, it has been shown in pancreatic cancer cells that glutamine-derived pyruvate plays a significant role in redox homeostasis.
evidence: Reference to findings in pancreatic cancer cells

claim: Two cell-autonomous, primary deficiencies occur in AMI patient-derived ECs: (1) a strong proton coupling in the mitochondrial membrane that results in excess ROS production, countered by enhanced NADPH and glutathione levels, driven by a glycolysis-to-PPP shunt and an enhanced glutamine metabolism; and (2) a switch in carbon source preference from glucose to glutamine.
source: Collectively, our observations and evidence by others suggest the occurrence of two cell-autonomous, primary deficiencies in AMI patient-derived ECs, namely (1) a strong proton coupling in the mitochondrial membrane that results in excess ROS production, countered by enhanced NADPH and glutathione levels, driven by a glycolysis-to-PPP shunt and an enhanced glutamine metabolism; and (2) a switch in carbon source preference from glucose to glutamine, possibly as an adaptive mechanism aimed at potentiating the production of glutathione, while employing alternative pyruvate-to-lactate conversion pathways that replenish NAD+, thus maintaining a viable redox homeostasis (Kerk et al., 2022).
evidence: Inference drawn from the collective data presented in the study, with citation to Kerk et al., 2022

claim: Primary dysfunctions in mitochondria, from either inherited or acquired genetic defects, have been suggested as underlying causes of atherogenic pathologies.
source: Primary dysfunctions in mitochondria, from either inherited or acquired genetic defects, have been suggested as underlying causes of atherogenic pathologies (Dabravolski et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dabravolski et al., 2022

claim: A possible intervention to revert the observed mitochondrial dysfunction would be the use of pharmacological uncouplers to mitigate ROS production and the accompanying metabolic reprogramming.
source: Independent of the original insult, a possible intervention to revert the observed mitochondrial dysfunction would be the use of pharmacological uncouplers to mitigate ROS production and the accompanying metabolic reprogramming (Cadenas, 2018).
evidence: Speculative suggestion based on the observed mitochondrial dysfunction, with citation to Cadenas, 2018

claim: Knockout of the uncoupling protein UCP1 caused vascular dysfunction, atherogenesis, and NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL1-β-dependent inflammation, relieved by re-expression of UCP1 or treatment of animals with chemical uncouplers.
source: Relevantly, knockout of the uncoupling protein UCP1 caused vascular dysfunction, atherogenesis, and NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL1-β-dependent inflammation, relieved by re-expression of UCP1 or treatment of animals with chemical uncouplers (Gu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gu et al., 2021

claim: AMIECs display impaired growth, migration, and tubulogenesis.
source: AMI-derived endothelial cells (AMIECs) display impaired growth, migration, and tubulogenesis.
evidence: Summary statement from the Abstract based on experimental data

claim: AMIECs displayed augmented ROS and glutathione intracellular content.
source: Metabolically, AMIECs displayed augmented ROS and glutathione intracellular content, with a diminished glucose consumption coupled to high lactate production.
evidence: Summary statement from the Abstract based on experimental data

claim: AMIECs displayed diminished glucose consumption coupled to high lactate production.
source: Metabolically, AMIECs displayed augmented ROS and glutathione intracellular content, with a diminished glucose consumption coupled to high lactate production.
evidence: Summary statement from the Abstract based on experimental data

claim: In AMIECs, PFKFB3 protein levels were downregulated.
source: In AMIECs, while PFKFB3 protein levels of were downregulated, PFKFB4 levels were upregulated, suggesting a shunting of glycolysis towards the pentose phosphate pathway, supported by upregulation of G6PD.
evidence: Summary statement from the Abstract based on experimental data

claim: In AMIECs, PFKFB4 levels were upregulated.
source: In AMIECs, while PFKFB3 protein levels of were downregulated, PFKFB4 levels were upregulated, suggesting a shunting of glycolysis towards the pentose phosphate pathway, supported by upregulation of G6PD.
evidence: Summary statement from the Abstract based on experimental data

claim: The downregulation of PFKFB3 and upregulation of PFKFB4 in AMIECs suggests a shunting of glycolysis towards the pentose phosphate pathway.
source: In AMIECs, while PFKFB3 protein levels of were downregulated, PFKFB4 levels were upregulated, suggesting a shunting of glycolysis towards the pentose phosphate pathway, supported by upregulation of G6PD.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed expression patterns of PFKFB3 and PFKFB4

claim: G6PD was upregulated in AMIECs.
source: In AMIECs, while PFKFB3 protein levels of were downregulated, PFKFB4 levels were upregulated, suggesting a shunting of glycolysis towards the pentose phosphate pathway, supported by upregulation of G6PD.
evidence: Summary statement from the Abstract based on experimental data

claim: The glutaminolytic enzyme GLS was upregulated in AMIECs.
source: Furthermore, the glutaminolytic enzyme GLS was upregulated in AMIECs, providing an explanation for the increase in glutathione content.
evidence: Summary statement from the Abstract based on experimental data

claim: The upregulation of GLS in AMIECs provides an explanation for the increase in glutathione content.
source: Furthermore, the glutaminolytic enzyme GLS was upregulated in AMIECs, providing an explanation for the increase in glutathione content.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed upregulation of GLS and increased glutathione content

claim: AMIECs displayed a significantly higher mitochondrial membrane potential than control ECs.
source: Finally, AMIECs displayed a significantly higher mitochondrial membrane potential than control ECs, which, together with high ROS levels, suggests a coupled mitochondrial activity.
evidence: Summary statement from the Abstract based on experimental data

claim: The significantly higher mitochondrial membrane potential in AMIECs, together with high ROS levels, suggests a coupled mitochondrial activity.
source: Finally, AMIECs displayed a significantly higher mitochondrial membrane potential than control ECs, which, together with high ROS levels, suggests a coupled mitochondrial activity.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed high mitochondrial membrane potential and high ROS levels

claim: High mitochondrial proton coupling underlies the high production of ROS in AMIECs, balanced by PPP- and glutaminolysis-driven synthesis of glutathione, as a primary, cell-autonomous abnormality driving EC dysfunction in AMI.
source: We suggest that high mitochondrial proton coupling underlies the high production of ROS, balanced by PPP- and glutaminolysis-driven synthesis of glutathione, as a primary, cell-autonomous abnormality driving EC dysfunction in AMI.
evidence: Inference drawn from the collective data presented in the study
